card.hook: Try fitting a 237-metre tower into your phone screen and you'll soon see the problem: it's huge. The good news is that it's perfectly symmetrical, so a straight-on shot looks great with very little effort.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac Defilad, right in front of the palace's main facade and lined up with the middle of the tower. Face the palace, so the tower rises in a clean line with modern high-rises on either side.
card.zoom: If you're close, use zoom 0.5x to get the whole tower in. Step back and 1x does the job. Use zoom 2x to 5x for the clock faces, the statues by the entrance or the spire.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the spire up with the middle vertical line, then tap the tower and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or blue hour, when the tower stands out against the sky. Since 2010 it has been lit by LED lights that can change colour, so an evening shot can look very different from a daytime one.
card.selfie_here: Head for the fountain on the park square below the tower in Plac Defilad, and take your selfie with the palace rising behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a bit low so the tower fits over your shoulder. You can also try the Złote Tarasy side, just west of the palace, with the tower in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand far back across Plac Defilad while you stand in front of the main facade, so the whole tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks may be restricted inside theatres, temporary exhibitions and performances in the complex, so check the signs at each entrance. Inside attractions like the 30th-floor terrace, theatres and museums may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the statues of Copernicus and Mickiewicz by the main entrance and get one of them in your shot with the tower rising behind.
card.good_to_know: The palace was built between 1952 and 1955 and designed by the Soviet architect Lev Rudnev. He took inspiration from American art deco skyscrapers and added Polish details, like parapets modelled on Renaissance houses. At about 237 metres, it's still the second tallest building in Poland. Look up near the top for four clock faces, each 6.3 metres across.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac Defilad, right in front of the palace's main facade and lined up with the middle of the tower. Face the palace, so the tower rises in a clean line with modern high-rises on either side.

card.hook: You're looking for a museum, but the building looks like a brick power station, because it used to be one. That chunky brick front is your photo, so don't walk past it hunting for something fancier.
card.stand_here: Walk to the street-facing entrance at Grzybowska 79 in Wola. The phone icon marks the middle of the museum, not the door, so head for the front. Face the brick facade, with the entrance low in your frame and the sky and nearby towers above it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and entrance in one shot, then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the brickwork and the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the walls with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: We don't have a best hour for this one, so check the official site for current opening times. If the sky is bright, tap the brickwork and drag the slider to darker so the bricks keep their texture.
card.selfie_here: Try the forecourt in front of the brick building, by the entrance gate and the flagpoles on the left side of the facade. Use your front camera (zoom 0.5x if it has it), and put the flagpoles, the lawn and the building behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep the entrance clear so other visitors can get in and out. Inside, photos for personal use are generally allowed but flash is usually banned, and rules can vary by exhibition, so follow the staff signs. The museum is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

card.good_to_know: The Warsaw Uprising Museum tells the story of the 1944 uprising. It was set up as an institution in 1983 and opened on 31 July 2004, the 60th anniversary of the uprising. Inside there's a hall with a full-size B-24 Liberator. Outside, Freedom Park has a memorial wall of names, a replica of the Kubuś armoured car and more than 30 colourised photo posters.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the street-facing entrance at Grzybowska 79 in Wola. The phone icon marks the middle of the museum, not the door, so head for the front. Face the brick facade, with the entrance low in your frame and the sky and nearby towers above it.

card.hook: Plot twist: that glowing red castle was blown up in 1944, and you're looking at the rebuild. The open square in front gives it plenty of room to show off.
card.stand_here: Stand on Plac Zamkowy, at the edge near Krakowskie Przedmieście or on the Old Town side of the square. The castle lies to the east, so face east with Sigismund's Column in front of you and the Old Town rooftops behind.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the castle, the column and the sky into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details like the facade or the rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the column on one third of the frame, then tap the red facade and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Come at blue hour, when the castle is lit up and glowing. Dawn gives you a much emptier square. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the steps at the base of Sigismund's Column with your back to the castle facade and the square in front of you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the red castle fits over your shoulder. For a quieter option, try the garden lawns below the river-side facade, with the castle behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on ulica Świętojańska looking toward the castle, while you stand in front of the red facade on the square.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the castle, photos are allowed without flash, though some exhibitions don't allow photos at all, so check on the day. Visitor guides say selfie sticks are banned inside, so keep yours in your bag. Drone flying is typically restricted around the castle.
card.challenge: Get the whole long castle in the frame without it leaning, then take one more with Sigismund's Column sitting neatly on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: The castle began in the 14th century as a home for the Dukes of Masovia. Under Sigismund III Vasa in the early 1600s it grew into the Mannerist-Baroque building you see now. After it was blown up in September 1944, it was rebuilt from surviving fragments, documents and rescued artworks, and the interiors reopened in 1984.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Plac Zamkowy, at the edge near Krakowskie Przedmieście or on the Old Town side of the square. The castle lies to the east, so face east with Sigismund's Column in front of you and the Old Town rooftops behind.

card.hook: Most stadiums look like concrete bowls. This one is dressed up as a waving Polish flag, and it works best when you step back far enough to see the whole thing at once.
card.stand_here: Stand on Most Poniatowskiego (the Poniatowski Bridge), coming in from the bridge's side, and face the stadium. You'll see the full front with the bridge running alongside it, which is the classic view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole curved front and the bridge fit in one frame. Then try zoom 2x (some phones go to 3x) for a tighter shot of the red-and-white panels and the spire. Zoom 0.5x is only worth it if you walk much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the stadium's long edge up with a horizontal line, then tap the stadium and slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the red keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before noon, when the light hits the east-facing panels. Traffic on the bridge can photobomb you, so take a few shots in a row and wait for a gap.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Poniatowski Bridge walkway over the Vistula. Face away from the stadium so it sits behind you, use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it), and tilt the phone so the long curve fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Wisłostrada has a street view point where the bridge and stadium both fit in the frame, so you could ask a passer-by there, but check the spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for event-day closures around the stadium before you go. The bridge view is from a public road, so keep an eye on the traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get the bridge's edge leading your eye straight to the stadium, with not a single van in the shot?
card.good_to_know: The stadium was built between 2008 and November 2011, on the site of the old 10th-Anniversary Stadium. It seats 58,580 for football, which makes it the largest football arena in Poland, and it hosted matches at UEFA Euro 2012. The roof hangs from a tall central spire that rises about 124 metres above the Vistula.

card.hook: Four stone lions, one bronze horse and a very long, very pale palace that won't fit in your photo unless you back right up. Cross the street and it all clicks into place.
card.stand_here: Stand on Krakowskie Przedmieście, opposite the palace across the boulevard near Hotel Bristol, a few steps back from the façade. Face the palace so the whole colonnaded front fits in the frame, with the Poniatowski statue in the forecourt.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from across the boulevard. If the pavement is busy and you can't step back any further, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statue, the lions and the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line them up with the palace's columns and roofline, and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is best. The street is quiet and the light falls across the front from the east. Late afternoon gives you softer light.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the street-side pavement next to the bronze Prince Józef Poniatowski horse statue, with the palace façade behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the horse and the columns both fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the boulevard, roughly opposite Hotel Bristol, while you stand by the statue, so they can fit the whole façade and the statue in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside are fine, but please don't block the gate. The palace is a security zone, so stay outside the perimeter and follow the guards' instructions.
card.challenge: Get the horse, the columns and all four lions into your set of photos, with the palace standing perfectly straight in at least one.
card.good_to_know: The palace began in 1643 as a grand private mansion. The architect Chrystian Piotr Aigner shaped the classical look you see today from 1818, adding the colonnade, balustrade and the stone statues along the top. It has been home to Poland's head of state since July 1994, and it came through the 1944 Warsaw Uprising intact.

card.hook: Walk through the entrance gate and there it is, a big yellow-and-white palace sitting dead centre in front of you, like it's been waiting all day for your photo. Guides call this the most photographed palace view in Poland, and you'll see why in about two seconds.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole façade in. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x. Then go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved trophies and emblems.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the middle of the palace with the centre line, then tap the façade and slide it a little darker so the pale yellow and white don't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a bright day when the sun isn't straight overhead, like mid-morning or late afternoon. Early is best if you want fewer people in the courtyard.
card.selfie_here: Head round to the garden side of the palace and stand beside one of the large garden statues, with the façade behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low, so the statue is up front and the palace fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by in the front courtyard, stand in front of the main building, and ask them to step back and frame you with the palace behind.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed in the palace and park as long as you don't disturb other guests or endanger historic objects. Flash isn't allowed inside the palace, and some park and garden areas need a ticket.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the whole palace, then find three different royal details on the façade and zoom in on each one.
card.good_to_know: Wilanów Palace was built between 1677 and 1696 for King John III Sobieski, to a design by Augustyn Wincenty Locci. It came through the Second World War and reopened to the public in 1962. The museum dates from 1805, and around 3 million people visited in 2019, so expect company.

card.hook: It looks like a fortress that fought a hundred battles, but the Barbican only has one recorded fight to its name. That round brick bulge by the Old Town walls is a great subject for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Podwale, on the moat side, in the street below the walls. Face the round bastion so the gateway rises up beside the old moat.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bastion, the gateway and the moat into one frame. Then try 1x for a natural look. Go to 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the brick texture and the tops of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the moat in the bottom third and the bastion in the middle, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light is best for the view from Podwale. For a warm glow on the brick towers, try the Nowomiejska side around sunset.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Podwale pavement beside the old moat, with the Barbican walls behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so the whole bastion fits over your shoulder. For a sunset selfie, try the Nowomiejska side with the brick towers behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Podwale by the moat and frame you against the Barbican, which is the classic view from this side.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go into the exhibition inside, check the signs or ask staff about photo rules, including flash. The exhibition only runs in some seasons, and the walkway on top depends on the weather, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same Barbican shot from three spots (Podwale, Plac Krasińskich and Nowomiejska), then pick your winner later over coffee.
card.good_to_know: The Barbican was built in 1540 to a design by Jan Baptist the Venetian. It's about 14 metres wide and 15 metres high from the bottom of the moat, and it juts out around 30 metres from the walls. Most of what you see is a rebuild from 1952 to 1954, made after wartime destruction using old etchings as a guide and bricks salvaged from buildings in Nysa and Wrocław.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Podwale, on the moat side, in the street below the walls. Face the round bastion so the gateway rises up beside the old moat.

card.hook: Picture a pale palace sitting on its own little island, with trees around it and water all the way to your feet. Warsaw doesn't get much more postcard than this, and you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Agrykola bridge, the one carrying Agrykola street over the park water, and look south-east across the water. The palace faces you from its island. The exact spot on the bridge can differ from what you expect, so check the map.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the palace, water and trees all fit. Then try 2x, or a bit higher if your phone has it, to bring the facade closer without moving. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground water, and keep the palace near the middle so it doesn't stretch at the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the palace on an upper line and let the water fill the bottom third, keeping the horizon level.
card.best_time: Early morning is a good bet. The park is quieter and the water is often calmer, which gives you a reflection. A bright, overcast day works too because it keeps the light even on the pale walls.
card.selfie_here: Head for the bridge south of the palace, reached by following the western shore down toward it. Use the front camera, turn around so the palace is behind you with its reflection in the water, and try 0.5x if you want more of the scene in. The sources disagree on the best bridge, so the bridge on the palace's north side is a second option. Check both on the map.
card.ask_someone: At the Amphitheatre lawn or path, ask someone nearby to take your photo so the palace and Amphitheatre sit in the same frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The park and the palace exterior are free to enter, but going inside is ticketed. Photo rules inside vary, especially for flash, so check at the entrance.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the palace small and the water big, then one with it big and the water small, and see which one you'd put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: The palace began as a Baroque bathhouse, built between 1683 and 1689 for Prince Stanisław Herakliusz Lubomirski. King Stanisław August Poniatowski bought the estate in 1764 and turned it into his summer residence, and it had its neoclassical look by the 1790s. German forces set it on fire in 1944, and it reopened to the public in 1960 after being rebuilt.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Agrykola bridge, the one carrying Agrykola street over the park water, and look south-east across the water. The palace faces you from its island. The exact spot on the bridge can differ from what you expect, so check the map.

card.hook: Picture a wide, open square with a row of stone arches and a small flame glowing under them. That's your first shot, and it's a good one. The garden is right behind it, so you get two pictures for one short stroll.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac Marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego, in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier arcade, and face the arches. The middle of the garden is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot from the square.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and step back a little so both the arches and the square fit. If you can't back up far enough, tap 0.5x. Save 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the guard or for details of the statues in the garden.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the columns straight, tap the arches, and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Morning is calmer, so you'll get fewer people in your shot. Late afternoon is softer on the stone. The guard changes every hour, so time your visit if you want that little bit of action.
card.selfie_here: Walk into the garden and find the sundial in the middle of the park. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the main avenue of statues behind you. The Marconi fountain near the southern corner of the park is another good backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The Tomb is a place of remembrance, so keep well clear of the guards, and be aware that mourners may be present. The garden is a public park open from dawn to dusk, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the arches, the flame and a guard all in one straight, gridline-perfect shot without a single lean?
card.good_to_know: The Saxon Garden is Warsaw's oldest public park. It opened to the public on 27 May 1727, which made it one of the first parks in the world anyone could walk into. It began as a formal Baroque garden and was later reshaped into a softer English-style park. About 20 of its old sandstone statues survive.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac Marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego, in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier arcade, and face the arches. The middle of the garden is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot from the square.

card.hook: Everything on Nowy Świat looks gloriously old, and nearly all of it is a very convincing rebuild. The rooflines march off into the distance like they're showing you the way.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Krakowskie Przedmieście and Nowy Świat, at the south end by the Copernicus monument in front of Staszic Palace. Point your phone south and the street runs away from you with the statue in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic junction view. Switch to 0.5x if you want the whole statue and the facades on both sides, and keep the statue away from the edge so it doesn't look stretched. Try 2x to squeeze the buildings closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the building edges stay nice and upright, then put the statue to one side instead of dead centre.
card.best_time: Early morning or the golden hour before sunset usually gives softer light and fewer people. For a second view, go to Plac Trzech Krzyży at the far end in the early evening, when the street lamps are lit.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the junction where Nowy Świat meets Krakowskie Przedmieście, just across the Świętokrzyska intersection. A photo guide calls it an iconic view, and it's where the street changes its name. For a calmer backdrop, stand on the pavement between Foksal Street and Three Crosses Square with the facades behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so more of the street fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public street, but check for events or closures before you go, as it can be pedestrian-only on some summer weekends.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the statue off to one side and a café table in the corner, then wait for a gap and grab a second one with just the facades.
card.good_to_know: Nowy Świat is part of the Royal Route, which links the Royal Castle and Old Town with the old royal residence at Wilanów. Almost all of it was destroyed in the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. It was rebuilt to look as it did in the early 19th century, when stone and brick buildings of about three storeys replaced the earlier wooden manors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Krakowskie Przedmieście and Nowy Świat, at the south end by the Copernicus monument in front of Staszic Palace. Point your phone south and the street runs away from you with the statue in front.

card.hook: Those pastel houses look like they've been standing for 400 years, but they were rebuilt between 1948 and 1953 to look as they did in the 17th century. Either way, they make one of the best photo backdrops in Warsaw.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rynek Starego Miasta (the Old Town Market Place), in the northwest corner of the square. Face into the square so the whole sweep of townhouses is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to squeeze the whole ring of facades into one shot. Switch to 1x for the Mermaid with the houses behind her, and try 2x for details on the facades (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the houses up with the vertical lines, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Go from dawn to 8 a.m. if you want the square almost empty. Late afternoon is your pick for warmer light on the facades.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the middle of the square and stand next to the bronze Mermaid (Syrenka) statue, with the coloured townhouses behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if the houses don't fit.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by in the northwest corner, ask them to shoot at 0.5x, and stand in front of the townhouses so the whole sweep fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space you can visit at any time. The museums on its sides are separate, so check their official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Get the Mermaid big in the foreground with a row of colourful houses standing perfectly straight behind her.
card.good_to_know: This square is the oldest part of Warsaw's Old Town and dates from the late 13th century. It was the heart of the whole city until the end of the 18th century. The bronze Mermaid by Konstanty Hegel has been the city's symbol since 1855, and the square is about 90 by 73 metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rynek Starego Miasta (the Old Town Market Place), in the northwest corner of the square. Face into the square so the whole sweep of townhouses is in front of you.

card.hook: Bronze insurgents come charging out of a collapsing building, and the whole scene looks like a film still. You'll want to see it from the front first, then work your way round.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac Krasińskich (Krasiński Square), in front of the monument, and face the bronze group with the Supreme Court building behind it. The monument is on the square's southern side, so the court building makes a calm, plain backdrop.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole group in one frame. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for faces and details in the bronze. Walk up close, hold your phone low at 0.5x and shoot upwards so the figures seem to surge over you.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze, then slide the brightness down a little so the dark metal keeps its detail against the bright sky and building.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or when it's overcast. Harsh midday sun washes out the detail in the sculpture.
card.selfie_here: Crouch beside the sewer hatch cover at the base of the monument, with the bronze figures behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it. Check the framing on the spot, because this is a low-angle shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square facing the monument, so the whole group sits in front of the Supreme Court building, while you stand near the monument.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed for personal use. This is a memorial, so respect any ceremonies taking place and give other visitors space.
card.challenge: Crouch down and read what's cast into the manhole cover ("GLORY TO THE HEROES"), then get one shot with the hatch sharp and the bronze fighters rushing behind it.
card.good_to_know: This monument remembers the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 and was unveiled on 1 August 1989, the 45th anniversary of the uprising's outbreak. It stands about 10 metres tall. The larger part shows insurgents running into combat, and the smaller part shows fighters climbing down a manhole, a nod to the sewer journey that took thousands of insurgents out of the Old Town in September 1944, starting from this square. Jacek Budyn designed it and Wincenty Kućma sculpted it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac Krasińskich (Krasiński Square), in front of the monument, and face the bronze group with the Supreme Court building behind it. The monument is on the square's southern side, so the court building makes a calm, plain backdrop.

card.hook: A bronze king in full armour, a cross in one hand and a sabre in the other, towers over Castle Square with a big red-brick castle behind him. He's got the best seat in Warsaw, and he's very easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac Zamkowy, a few steps back from the base of the column, and face the Royal Castle facade. The column will rise in front of the red-brick castle, with the Old Town roofline beyond.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the column and castle together. If you're close and want the whole tall column and the square in one shot, try 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) gets you in tight on the king and the four eagles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the column on one of the vertical lines, then tap the column and drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the bronze.
card.best_time: Go before 9 a.m. for fewer tour groups, or in the late afternoon for warm light on the castle facade. Summer midday is the busiest time.
card.selfie_here: Try the broken pieces of the original column shaft, displayed near the Royal Castle entrance, a few metres from the column's base. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up so the column sits over your shoulder. This spot is our best guess, so check the angle when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand a few steps back out across the square, so the whole column and the castle facade fit, while you pose near the base.
card.rules_and_safety: The cobblestones are uneven and can be slippery after rain or snow, so watch your step as you back up for the shot.
card.challenge: Find all four eagles on the column, then zoom in and get a clear shot of one of them.
card.good_to_know: The column first went up in 1644, when King Władysław IV Vasa honoured his father, Sigismund III Vasa, who moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw in 1596. The Germans brought it down on 1 September 1944, during the Warsaw Uprising. The statue was repaired and set on a new granite column in 1949, a short way from the original spot, and the square is part of Warsaw's UNESCO-listed Historic Centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac Zamkowy, a few steps back from the base of the column, and face the Royal Castle facade. The column will rise in front of the red-brick castle, with the Old Town roofline beyond.

card.hook: Krakowskie Przedmieście never stops moving, but the Holy Cross Church facade just sits there, calm and perfectly symmetrical, like it's ignoring the whole rush. Come back in the evening, when it's lit up against a deep blue sky.
card.stand_here: Cross to the far pavement from the church, on Krakowskie Przedmieście opposite the University of Warsaw campus, and look north. Let the lit facade fill the middle of your frame and pick your exact spot by eye along the pavement.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole facade plus some of the street. Tap 2x when you want the two towers to fill the picture. Skip 0.5x unless you walk right up to the church.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lit facade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays deep blue and the lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Evening, when the sky turns a rich blue and the church is lit. As the light fades, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body, or lean on a lamp post, to keep it sharp.
card.selfie_here: Go up to the raised terrace between the two staircases at the entrance (Krakowskie Przedmieście 3), turn on the front camera and let the towers rise behind your shoulder. Or stand in front of the statue of Christ carrying the cross, with the church entrance behind it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Krakowskie Przedmieście pavement a few steps back from the church front, while you stand by the entrance, so the street frames the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the pavement, because the boulevard is busy with traffic. It's an active church. Photos inside are generally fine without flash, but not during services or at certain memorials, so follow any posted signs.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight on your gridlines, with one stranger walking past in the street lights, and you've got a proper city shot.
card.good_to_know: The main building went up between 1679 and 1696, designed by Józef Szymon Bellotti, and the towers got their late Baroque tops in the early 18th century. Inside, a pillar holds the urn with Frédéric Chopin's heart. The church was badly damaged in 1944 and blown up in January 1945, then rebuilt between 1945 and 1953 in a simpler form.

card.hook: This monument has two completely different faces, and most people only photograph one. On the west side, a bronze crowd of insurgents surges forward. Walk round the back and it's all quiet stone.
card.stand_here: Stand on plac Bohaterów Getta Warszawskiego, right at the phone icon on the map. Face the bronze group with the tall stone wall rising behind it, and the POLIN museum is opposite.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole monument. If you're close and the top gets cut off, drop to 0.5x to fit the full height and the plaza. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the faces and figures in the relief.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bronze group slightly off-centre and keep the phone level so the vertical edges stay straight; if the sky is bright, tap the bronze figures and slide it a little darker so the bronze keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day is best. The lower light makes stronger shadows that bring out the detail in the relief.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open square between the monument and POLIN, near the middle, with the monument at your back. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the monument as a wide backdrop over your shoulder, not a close-up pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the POLIN side of the square facing the monument, then stand between them and the monument so the whole wall fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine at this outdoor monument, but it's a solemn place, so don't climb or sit on it, avoid posing in ways that feel disrespectful, and stand back during ceremonies. Wait for a gap between visitors rather than asking anyone to move. The square's surface can be uneven in places, so go slowly with a wheelchair or stroller.
card.challenge: Get two shots with one idea: the bronze side with its vertical edges dead straight, then the quiet stone relief on the other side. Two faces, two moods.
card.good_to_know: The monument stands where the first armed clash of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising took place. It was unveiled on 19 April 1948, is about 11 metres tall and was sculpted by Nathan Rapoport. Part of the stone is labradorite from German supplies ordered by Albert Speer in 1942 for planned Nazi monuments.

card.hook: Chopin is sitting under a willow in Łazienki Park, and somehow he's got a twin in the pond. That still water does half the work for you, so one quick shot gets the statue, the tree and the reflection.
card.stand_here: Go to the front of the monument in Łazienki Park and stand right at the subject, facing the sculpture across the pond. Once you can see the water and the willow, you're in the right place.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the statue, the willow and the reflection in one go. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the bronze and the words on the plinth.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one third of the frame and let the pond fill the bottom so the reflection comes along for the ride.
card.best_time: Early morning is the sweet spot, with fewer people and calmer light. Sunday summer concerts fill the benches and lawn, so come before or after them if you want a quiet frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the rim of the red sandstone pond, off to one side, so the bronze figure and the willow rise up behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want more of the scene in. Or take a close one among the rose beds with the statue right behind you.
card.ask_someone: The pavement on Aleje Ujazdowskie, across from the Łazienki gate, shows the whole statue and willow, so hand over your phone there and ask for a full-length shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the park and around the monument, but be mindful of other visitors. Conservation works have been reported, so look for scaffolding before you plan your shot.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap between breezes and catch the reflection with no ripples at all. Patience wins here.
card.good_to_know: The Chopin Monument is a seated bronze figure of the composer, set beneath a stylised willow. Guides often call it one of Warsaw's most photographed sights. It's free to view, and you can also glimpse it through the park gate from Aleje Ujazdowskie.

card.hook: Most people stand at the water's edge and shoot straight at the fountains. Walk up the rise instead and you get the whole show laid out below you, with Old Town rooftops and church towers behind it like a painted backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand on the raised ground at the edge of Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej, above the fountains. Face the water so the fountains are below you and the Old Town skyline sits behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole display and the skyline in one frame. Switch to 1x for a tidier view, then try 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to pick out the church towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountains on the lower third and the rooftops and towers along the upper third, then tap the fountains and drag the slider a little darker so bright water and lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go for the last light before sunset, when the Old Town rooftops catch the glow. On show evenings (Friday and Saturday, May to September) arrive early, because the best spots fill up.
card.selfie_here: Try the small hill at the edge of the park, on the gentle rise behind the fountains. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone so the Old Town rooftops are over your shoulder as the light fades. Treat it as a great viewpoint rather than a guaranteed fountain-behind-you selfie.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the main fountain and ask a passer-by to step back and frame you with the whole fountain complex and show behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos and videos are generally fine, but a photo ban can apply during performances if it's announced, so be ready to put your phone away. Professional or commercial shoots may need permits. Keep an eye on children near the water's edge, especially after dark.
card.challenge: Can you get the fountains in the bottom third, the church towers in the top third, and a stranger in the middle wondering what you're doing?
card.good_to_know: The Multimedia Fountain Park is a set of fountains with a projection screen, set below the escarpment, and the park is free. Shows run only on Friday and Saturday evenings from May to September. Winter illuminations were listed for 2025/2026 only, so check whether they return. For a street-level view, try ulica Rybaki, where the fountains and screen sit against the church silhouettes.

card.hook: Some church fronts look like they've been ironed, and St. Anne's is one of them. The pale, tidy facade right next to Castle Square is made for a perfectly balanced photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Krakowskie Przedmieście, on the street directly in front of the church's main facade, and face the church so the doorway is in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front, straight on. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all in, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Evangelist statues above the door.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the central doorway up with the middle vertical line, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when there are fewer people around Castle Square and your shots come out cleaner. The church is closed to visitors during Mass, so plan around that.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the open paved square in front of the facade, on the Castle Square side, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the building in, and keep the facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on Castle Square, far enough to fit the whole building in, while you pose in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the church and from the bell tower, but the church is in regular religious use, so be considerate and skip the flash. The bell tower has 147 steps, and the top can be wet, icy and very windy, so take care in bad weather.
card.challenge: Get the doorway exactly on the middle gridline, then zoom in and find one of the Four Evangelists without moving your feet.
card.good_to_know: The church was founded in 1454 by Duchess Anna Fiodorowna for Bernardine friars, and it has been rebuilt several times since. The Neoclassical front you see today dates from 1788 and was designed by Chrystian Piotr Aigner. The Evangelist statues were carved by Jakub Monaldi and Franciszek Pinck.

card.hook: One dark bronze man, holding a compass, stands against a very long, very pale palace, and it looks like a poster for Warsaw. Copernicus is the star here, and the palace is his backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the front of the pedestal on Krakowskie Przedmieście and face the Staszic Palace. If you walk west to reach the front of the pedestal, you'll land in the classic spot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the statue and the palace facade together. Then try 2x for a tighter shot of the figure and his compass, and save 0.5x for the whole square with Copernicus looking small.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a little if the pale facade looks washed out or the bronze looks too dark.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is calmer, so you'll have a better shot at a clear frame. Midday crowds mean you may need a bit of patience.
card.selfie_here: Try standing on the bronze solar-system model at the foot of the statue, with Copernicus behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze him in, and hold the phone a bit low so he stays over your shoulder. We couldn't confirm anyone else has taken a selfie right here, so you'd be a trailblazer.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to step back a few steps on Krakowskie Przedmieście so the whole monument fits in the frame with the Staszic Palace behind it, while you stand by the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public space, free to reach on foot at any hour.
card.challenge: Get three shots: one wide with the palace, one close on the compass and armillary sphere, and one of the Latin inscription on the east face of the pedestal.
card.good_to_know: Bertel Thorvaldsen designed the statue in 1822, and it was finished in 1830 with money from public donations and from Stanisław Staszic himself. The Germans took it away after the 1944 Warsaw Uprising but had to retreat before they could melt it down. It came back in July 1945 and was unveiled again in 1949.

card.hook: Picture a calm, sand-coloured building with the word Polin printed across its glass in both Latin and Hebrew letters. Across the street, a memorial keeps it company, so this is a photo stop that asks you to slow down.

card.selfie_here: Use the paved plot between the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes and the museum. The grass strip in front of the glass wall, near the tree, also works if you like the reflections.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the paved plot facing the museum, roughly 45 m from the main entrance, so the whole building fits in the frame with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum faces a memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, so please take photos with respect. Inside, photography is for personal use with no flash, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the curved stone wall leads your eye straight to the entrance, then take one shot with nobody in it. Patience is the whole game.
card.good_to_know: The museum stands in Muranów, the prewar Jewish quarter of Warsaw, on the site of the former Warsaw Ghetto. Finnish architects Rainer Mahlamäki and Ilmari Lahdelma designed it, and it opened on 19 April 2013. The core exhibition followed on 28 October 2014.
